transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... it's actually been really embarrassing lately at work. I'm a jeweler, you see, and I work mostly with precious stones and custom metal settings, which requires a lot of precision. I've always been good at the precision part, the hands-on part at the bench, but lately, the talking part is just... it's getting completely away from me. 

Like, just the other day, a customer came in and asked me a very simple question. They just wanted to know when their ring repair would be ready. It was a simple prong retipping, nothing major, it usually just takes a few days. But instead of just saying 'Thursday,' my answer... well, my answer started going off about the supplier invoices, because the gold wire shipment was delayed, and then somehow that reminded me of the delivery truck driving through the mud, which got me talking about the garden soil I just bought for my raised beds at home—I'm trying to grow tomatoes this year, Roma tomatoes mostly, because they're better for making sauce—and then, before I knew it, I was rambling on to this poor customer about my mortgage papers and how the bank's interest rates are affecting my ability to build a greenhouse in the backyard. 

And I could just see it in their eyes, you know? I could see them completely losing me, just staring at me like I was speaking a different language. And it's like my brain just connects all these things that make sense to me in the very moment I'm speaking, but when I say them out loud, it's this huge, confusing mess. I try to pull it back, but there's just so much detail that feels important to explain right then and there, and then I realize I haven't even answered their actual question about the ring. I just can't seem to get from point A to point B anymore without visiting the rest of the alphabet first, and I really can't afford to scare off my customers, so I figured I needed to come in and see what's going on with me.
Over the past few weeks, have you found that you are needing significantly less sleep than usual to feel fully rested and energized?

Oh, no. No, definitely not less sleep. If anything... well, I certainly wouldn't say I feel energized at all. Honestly, my sleep schedule has been pretty much the exact same as it always is. I usually try to get into bed by about 10:30 PM, right after I've watched a little television—I like to watch those antique restoration shows, you know, because it's sort of adjacent to what I do with jewelry, restoring old things, but without the pressure of it being *my* actual work. 

And I have this whole routine where I make a cup of chamomile tea, I steep it for exactly four minutes, no more or it gets too bitter, and then I read a bit. But I absolutely need my full eight hours. If I don't get my eight hours, my hands just aren't steady the next day. And when you're working with a jeweler's saw, or trying to set a tiny little half-carat sapphire into a white gold bezel, you absolutely cannot have shaky hands. One slip and you've scratched the stone or ruined the setting, and then you have to explain that to the client, which, as I was just saying, is something I'm really struggling with right now. 

So, no, I haven't been waking up early feeling ready to take on the world or anything like that. I just wake up at my normal time, around 6:30 AM, and I usually feel like I could easily use another hour or two in bed, to be perfectly honest with you. The alarm goes off, and I just stare at the ceiling for a good ten minutes before I can even convince myself to put my slippers on. So, no, definitely no extra energy or needing less sleep here.
Have you been hearing any sounds, voices, or whispers that other people around you do not seem to hear?

Well... yes, actually. It's... it's really strange that you ask that, because I was just thinking about how weird it's been getting at the shop. You know, my shop gets very, very quiet in the late afternoons, usually around 4:00 PM or so, because the foot traffic on my street just completely dies down after the lunch rush and before the evening commuters start walking by. And when it gets that quiet, you can hear a pin drop in there. 

But lately, when I'm just sitting quietly at my bench, I'll hear... well, I'll hear this woman's voice. She just sort of mutters my name, real low, and it always sounds like it's coming from the polishing room in the back. The polishing room has this heavy canvas curtain instead of a proper door, mostly to keep the dust contained—I use a lot of jeweler's rouge for polishing gold, and that red dust gets absolutely everywhere, all over the floor and the walls, if you aren't careful with the ventilation—so I can't actually see into the room from my main workbench. But I hear her mutter my name, clear as day, and it feels so incredibly real that I actually put down my tools, get off my stool, and walk all the way back there to check. I always think maybe a customer wandered into the back, or maybe someone needs help, but... there's never anyone there. It's just the polishing lathe sitting there in the dark. 

And it's not just the voice, either, which is the other thing that's been bothering me. Sometimes, I'll be up front doing paperwork or sketching out a new custom design, and out of nowhere, I will smell burning metal. Now, I know the smell of hot, melting metal very well—I use a Smith Little Torch with oxygen and propane for my soldering, and if you accidentally overheat a piece of sterling silver or scorch the flux, it has a very distinct, sharp, acrid smell. But I'll smell it when the torches are completely off. I mean, the tanks are closed tight at the main valves, the hoses are bled, the tips are cold, everything is completely shut down. But the smell is so strong and so present that I actually panic for a second. I'll drop my pencil and rush over to the soldering station just to check the valves and make sure I didn't leave a flame running or that the shop isn't about to catch fire. But everything is always perfectly fine and cold to the touch. It's just... it's really unsettling, having to constantly double-check my own senses like that when I'm just trying to get through my workday.

Have you ever experienced any sudden, brief periods where you felt confused, had a strange taste in your mouth, or felt like you were having a déjà vu experience right before you noticed these smells?

No, no, nothing like that at all. It's actually quite the opposite, really. I'm usually extremely clear-headed right before the smell hits. I have to be, you know? Like I was saying, the work I do requires intense concentration. Just the other day, when it happened, I was right in the middle of calculating the exact alloy mixture for a custom 14-karat rose gold cast. You really can't be confused or spacey when you're doing that kind of math, or the color of the gold will come out entirely wrong, it'll be too yellow or too copper-looking, and the client will be furious. So my mind is always very sharp right in those moments. 

And as for a strange taste... no, definitely not. I mean, unless you count the lingering taste of my afternoon tea. I usually switch from coffee to Earl Grey around 2:00 PM, and I always have it with just a tiny splash of oat milk—I find regular dairy milk coats my throat too much when I'm trying to talk to customers later in the day, which is already hard enough for me right now—but there's no weird metallic or sudden strange taste in my mouth at all, just the tea. 

And there's no déjà vu or anything like that, either. There's really no warning whatsoever. I'll just be sitting there on my stool, totally focused, maybe listening to the classical music station on the radio—I keep it on a very low volume, mostly just cellos and violins, because it helps me maintain a steady rhythm when I'm filing down rough edges on a new piece—and then, out of absolutely nowhere, just that sharp, acrid smell of burning metal. No weird feelings right before it, no confusion. It just suddenly smells exactly like my torch is running hot, and then I'm immediately jumping up out of my chair to go check the valves on the oxygen tank. So, no, none of those other things you mentioned.
Have you ever had any head injuries, seizures, or been diagnosed with any significant medical conditions, such as a tumor or a neurological disorder?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. I've never had a concussion or hit my head or anything. I'm generally a very cautious person, which, you know, you really have to be when you spend your days surrounded by heavy steel mandrels and sharp tools and spinning flex shafts. I actually wear an Optivisor—it's this magnifying headset that straps right around your forehead—pretty much all day so I can see the tiny prongs and the intricate details on the rings. Honestly, sometimes I joke that it acts like a little bumper for my head if I lean in too close to the bench pin, but no, no actual head injuries. 

And definitely no seizures or neurological issues. Thank goodness for that, because, like I was saying earlier about needing steady hands... if I had any kind of neurological problem or a tremor, or heaven forbid, a seizure while I was holding a torch or a high-speed drill rotating at ten thousand RPMs, it would be absolutely catastrophic. I could easily lose a finger, or I could completely destroy a piece of jewelry that's been in a client's family for generations, and I just couldn't live with that kind of guilt. 

As for tumors or any other major medical conditions, no, I've been very lucky in that department. I get my regular checkups, and my general practitioner—I've been seeing him for about fifteen years now, his office is just a few blocks down the street from my shop—he always says my blood pressure is perfect, my cholesterol is fine, and I've never had any major health scares. The absolute worst physical issue I get is just a little bit of stiffness in my neck and my shoulders from hunching over the workbench for hours on end, but I try to remember to do some stretches for that in the evenings. So, physically speaking, my brain and everything else should be in perfect working order. There's no medical reason for any of this, which is exactly why hearing that voice and smelling the metal when the torches are off is just so incredibly baffling to me.
When you hear that voice or smell the burning metal, do you believe that someone or something is actually trying to communicate with you or manipulate your shop environment?

No, no, I don't think the voice or the smell is a ghost or someone hiding in the walls trying to send me a secret message, if that's what you mean. I really just think my senses are playing tricks on me with the polishing room and the torches, as unsettling as it is. 

But... well, since you mention people having ulterior motives or doing things in the shop... I know it sounds odd, and I've been going back and forth on whether to even mention this because it sounds so strange out loud, but I’ve gotten absolutely convinced that some of the customers coming in aren't real customers at all. I really believe they are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss my payments. 

You see, we recently expanded and set up this beautiful new showroom area in the front of the store. We put in these gorgeous, custom-built cherry wood display cases with anti-glare glass and special daylight-balanced LED lighting to really make the diamonds and the colored gemstones sparkle. It was a huge investment, let me tell you, a really substantial loan to get it all done. And lately, these people will come in, and they just ask way, way too many questions about the new showroom. They’ll lean on the glass and ask how business is doing, if the new cases were expensive, how I'm managing the overhead with the street being so quiet... just incredibly pointed, intrusive questions that a normal person looking for a birthday gift simply wouldn't ask. 

My husband helps me with the bookkeeping on weekends, and he keeps telling me to just let it go. He says they’re only being friendly, that people are just curious and making small talk about the renovations. He tries to brush it off entirely. But I know what I'm seeing. They have this look in their eyes, like they're taking inventory, like they've been sent by someone to see if I'm going under and if they need to come repossess the cases or my inventory. It just makes me so incredibly anxious, having to stand there, put on a polite smile, and show them a sapphire pendant when I know exactly why they're really standing in my shop. So, no, I don't think anyone is manipulating my tools, but I definitely think people are coming in to monitor me.
How long have you been experiencing these periods of rambling speech and these specific concerns about the customers monitoring you?

Well, I don't know if I would call it rambling, Doctor. I just... I really believe it's important to be thorough and give you the whole picture. In my line of work, if you leave out a tiny detail, a stone falls out of its setting and a client is heartbroken. You have to look at every single facet. But to answer your question about the timeline... the worries about the customers watching us, and the voices, and that awful smell of burning metal, it all started around a year and eight months ago. 

I know the timeline exactly because it was right around the time we were finalizing the heavy paperwork for that showroom expansion loan I told you about. It was an incredibly stressful period. We had contractors coming in and out, tracking drywall dust everywhere, which is just an absolute nightmare when you're trying to keep a pristine workspace for polishing silver and gold. I was actually working on a custom platinum eternity band at the time—and platinum is notoriously difficult to work with, you know, it requires a much hotter torch than gold and it cools so quickly, so you really have to pay attention to what you're doing—and that's when I first started noticing that acrid smell when my torch wasn't even lit. 

And then the voice started shortly after that, just making those little comments while I was trying to concentrate on the platinum. And then, of course, once the new cherry wood cases were finally installed and the loan payments actually started coming due, that's when those specific "customers" started showing up to check on me and ask all those intrusive questions about our overhead. So yes, a year and eight months. My husband kept saying back then that it was just the stress of the renovation getting to me, but the construction has been done for well over a year now. The cases are settled, the daylight-balanced lights are perfectly angled, the shop looks beautiful, and yet these people are still coming in to monitor me, and I'm still smelling the metal and hearing the voice. So it really can't just be the stress of the construction, can it? Because twenty months is a very long time to be dealing with all of this, day in and day out, especially when you're trying to run a business and keep a polite smile on your face for the people who are actually there to buy jewelry.

I actually wear an Optivisor—it's this magnifying headset that straps right around your forehead—pretty much all day so I can see the tiny prongs and the intricate details on the rings. Honestly, sometimes I joke that it acts like a little bumper for my head if I lean in too close to the bench pin, but no, no actual head injuries. 

And definitely no seizures or neurological issues. Thank goodness for that, because, like I was saying earlier about needing steady hands... if I had any kind of neurological problem or a tremor, or heaven forbid, a seizure while I was holding a torch or a high-speed drill rotating at ten thousand RPMs, it would be absolutely catastrophic. I could easily lose a finger, or I could completely destroy a piece of jewelry that's been in a client's family for generations, and I just couldn't live with that kind of guilt. 

As for tumors or any other major medical conditions, no, I've been very lucky in that department. I get my regular checkups, and my general practitioner—I've been seeing him for about fifteen years now, his office is just a few blocks down the street from my shop—he always says my blood pressure is perfect, my cholesterol is fine, and I've never had any major health scares. The absolute worst physical issue I get is just a little bit of stiffness in my neck and my shoulders from hunching over the workbench for hours on end, but I try to remember to do some stretches for that in the evenings. So, physically speaking, my brain and everything else should be in perfect working order. There's no medical reason for any of this, which is exactly why hearing that voice and smelling the metal when the torches are off is just so incredibly baffling to me.

inference.note: The patient's denial of temporal lobe epilepsy symptoms (déjà vu, oral automatisms, or post-ictal confusion) makes F07.0 less likely, while the presence of specific, persistent, non-bizarre auditory and olfactory hallucinations in a clear sensorium warrants consideration of F22 (delusional disorder or related psychotic spectrum) alongside organic causes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient holds fixed, false beliefs or delusions about the source of these sensory experiences, which would help differentiate between a psychotic disorder (F22) and a medical/neurological etiology (F06.0/F06.8).
doctor.question: When you hear that voice or smell the burning metal, do you believe that someone or something is actually trying to communicate with you or manipulate your shop environment?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds odd, but I’ve gotten convinced some customers are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss payments, because they ask too many questions about the new showroom even after my husband says they’re only being friendly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about potential delusional beliefs related to my hallucinations, checking if I believe someone is trying to communicate with me or manipulate my environment, which maps to the Delusions symptom.

patient.answer:
No, no, I don't think the voice or the smell is a ghost or someone hiding in the walls trying to send me a secret message, if that's what you mean. I really just think my senses are playing tricks on me with the polishing room and the torches, as unsettling as it is. 

But... well, since you mention people having ulterior motives or doing things in the shop... I know it sounds odd, and I've been going back and forth on whether to even mention this because it sounds so strange out loud, but I’ve gotten absolutely convinced that some of the customers coming in aren't real customers at all. I really believe they are coming in just to check whether I’ll miss my payments. 

You see, we recently expanded and set up this beautiful new showroom area in the front of the store. We put in these gorgeous, custom-built cherry wood display cases with anti-glare glass and special daylight-balanced LED lighting to really make the diamonds and the colored gemstones sparkle. It was a huge investment, let me tell you, a really substantial loan to get it all done. And lately, these people will come in, and they just ask way, way too many questions about the new showroom. They’ll lean on the glass and ask how business is doing, if the new cases were expensive, how I'm managing the overhead with the street being so quiet... just incredibly pointed, intrusive questions that a normal person looking for a birthday gift simply wouldn't ask. 

My husband helps me with the bookkeeping on weekends, and he keeps telling me to just let it go. He says they’re only being friendly, that people are just curious and making small talk about the renovations. He tries to brush it off entirely. But I know what I'm seeing. They have this look in their eyes, like they're taking inventory, like they've been sent by someone to see if I'm going under and if they need to come repossess the cases or my inventory. It just makes me so incredibly anxious, having to stand there, put on a polite smile, and show them a sapphire pendant when I know exactly why they're really standing in my shop. So, no, I don't think anyone is manipulating my tools, but I definitely think people are coming in to monitor me.

inference.note: The patient's report of fixed, false beliefs regarding customers monitoring them, combined with auditory and olfactory hallucinations in the absence of neurological findings, points strongly toward a primary psychotic disorder. F06.0 and F06.8 are less likely given the lack of medical/neurological evidence.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's disorganized speech and beliefs have been present for at least six months to differentiate between F20.0 (Schizophrenia) and F22 (Delusional Disorder).
doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing these periods of rambling speech and these specific concerns about the customers monitoring you?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices, odd smells, and worries about customers watching us started around a year and eight months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of my disorganized speech (rambling) and delusions (concerns about customers monitoring me), which corresponds to the duration of my psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't know if I would call it rambling, Doctor. I just... I really believe it's important to be thorough and give you the whole picture. In my line of work, if you leave out a tiny detail, a stone falls out of its setting and a client is heartbroken. You have to look at every single facet. But to answer your question about the timeline... the worries about the customers watching us, and the voices, and that awful smell of burning metal, it all started around a year and eight months ago. 

I know the timeline exactly because it was right around the time we were finalizing the heavy paperwork for that showroom expansion loan I told you about. It was an incredibly stressful period. We had contractors coming in and out, tracking drywall dust everywhere, which is just an absolute nightmare when you're trying to keep a pristine workspace for polishing silver and gold. I was actually working on a custom platinum eternity band at the time—and platinum is notoriously difficult to work with, you know, it requires a much hotter torch than gold and it cools so quickly, so you really have to pay attention to what you're doing—and that's when I first started noticing that acrid smell when my torch wasn't even lit. 

And then the voice started shortly after that, just making those little comments while I was trying to concentrate on the platinum. And then, of course, once the new cherry wood cases were finally installed and the loan payments actually started coming due, that's when those specific "customers" started showing up to check on me and ask all those intrusive questions about our overhead. So yes, a year and eight months. My husband kept saying back then that it was just the stress of the renovation getting to me, but the construction has been done for well over a year now. The cases are settled, the daylight-balanced lights are perfectly angled, the shop looks beautiful, and yet these people are still coming in to monitor me, and I'm still smelling the metal and hearing the voice. So it really can't just be the stress of the construction, can it? Because twenty months is a very long time to be dealing with all of this, day in and day out, especially when you're trying to run a business and keep a polite smile on your face for the people who are actually there to buy jewelry.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms (persistent persecutory delusions regarding customers, auditory hallucinations, and olfactory hallucinations) have lasted for 20 months without the cognitive decline, negative symptoms, or disorganized behavior characteristic of schizophrenia (F20.0). The symptoms are centered on a specific delusional system, supporting a diagnosis of delusional disorder.

opening_question.question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent, non-bizarre delusional belief that customers are monitoring her financial status and business viability, lasting for over 20 months. While she reports auditory and olfactory phenomena, these occur in the context of high stress and do not dominate the clinical picture; the primary pathology is the fixed, organized delusional system regarding the customers. There is no evidence of a mood disorder, organic brain syndrome, or schizophrenia (no disorganized speech, catatonia, or negative symptoms).

Belief that customers ask intrusive questions to assess her business failure
Auditory hallucinations (hearing a woman mutter her name)
Olfactory hallucinations (smelling burning metal when no heat source is active)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms have been present for 20 months (1 year and 8 months), meeting the duration criterion for persistent delusional disorder.

Absence of schizophrenia criteria (no disorganization or negative symptoms)
